glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The writer urges his hearers to build on their foundation and go on to maturity, warns gravely that turning away from Christ after sharing in God’s great gifts leaves no way back to repentance, and then assures them of better things, resting their hope on God’s promise and oath and on Jesus, who has entered God’s presence for them.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 6 continues the appeal that began with the rebuke of dull hearing in 5:11–14. It closes by returning to Melchizedek (6:20), the subject chapter 7 explains.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which enters the Presence behind the veil, where the forerunner has entered for us, even Jesus, having become High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” (Hebrews 6:19–20)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The chapter opens with a call to grow: “let us go on to perfection” (6:1), that is, to maturity. The writer names six foundations: repentance from dead works, faith toward God, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. They remain the base of the Christian life, but believers are meant to build on them instead of laying them again.

Then comes one of the sternest warnings in Scripture. The writer describes people in the congregation who “were once enlightened,” tasted the heavenly gift, became “partakers of the Holy Spirit,” and tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come (6:4–5). These were real privileges. If such people deliberately turn away from Christ, it is impossible to renew them to repentance, “since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God, and put Him to an open shame” (6:6). Hebrews pictures two fields that drink the same rain. One bears useful crops and receives blessing from God; the other bears thorns and briers, is rejected and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned (6:7–8). The text does not settle what their inward standing had been, but it gives the consequence its full weight. This is settled rejection of the only Savior, not the stumbling of a believer who keeps looking to Christ.

The writer immediately turns to his hearers with warmth: “But, beloved, we are confident of better things concerning you” (6:9). God has not forgotten their love shown in serving the saints. Their hope rests on God Himself, who confirmed His promise to Abraham with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, “in which it is impossible for God to lie” (6:18), His people have strong encouragement. That hope is an anchor reaching into God’s presence, where Jesus has already gone ahead of them (6:19–20).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 6:1–3 — Go On to Maturity

The writer urges his hearers to move beyond the elementary teaching about Christ and go on to maturity. The foundation of repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, and eternal judgment remains, and with God’s help they will build on it.

Hebrews 6:4–8 — The Warning Against Falling Away

Those who have been enlightened, tasted God’s heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and experienced the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age cannot be renewed to repentance if they fall away, because they side with those who crucified the Son of God and expose Him to public shame. Two fields drink the same rain: the one that bears a useful crop receives God’s blessing, while the one that bears only thorns is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is to be burned.

Hebrews 6:9–12 — Confident of Better Things

Despite the warning, the writer is confident of better things for his hearers, things that belong with salvation. God remembers their love shown in serving the saints, and the writer wants them to keep the same diligence to the end and imitate those who inherit God’s promises through faith and patience.

Hebrews 6:13–18 — God’s Promise Confirmed by an Oath

God promised to bless Abraham and swore by Himself, and Abraham received what was promised after waiting patiently. God confirmed His purpose to His people with an oath as well as a promise, so that those who have fled to Him for refuge have strong encouragement, because God cannot lie.

Hebrews 6:19–20 — An Anchor Behind the Veil

Believers’ hope is a sure and steady anchor that reaches into God’s presence behind the veil. Jesus has already gone there ahead of them as forerunner and High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 6 holds warning and assurance together, and both must keep their full force. Turning deliberately from Christ after sharing in God’s gifts is a real danger with real consequences (6:4–8). Yet the same chapter calls its hearers “beloved,” remembers their love, and anchors their hope in God’s oath (6:9–18). A believer who is struggling with sin or fearful about his standing is not the person the warning describes; he is invited to cling to the hope set before him.

The chapter also shows where hope finds its hold. Hope does not rest on the strength of a person’s feelings. It is fastened to God’s unchanging promise and to Jesus, who has entered God’s presence on His people’s behalf (6:17–20).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Go on to maturity. Believers build on the foundation instead of laying it again (6:1–3).

The danger of turning away. Deliberate rejection of Christ after receiving His gifts leaves no way back to repentance (6:4–8).

Fruit that accompanies salvation. Love shown in serving the saints is fruit God remembers (6:9–12).

God’s promise and oath. God bound Himself by oath, and He cannot lie (6:13–18).

Hope anchored in God’s presence. Jesus has entered behind the veil as forerunner and High Priest (6:19–20).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Perfection (6:1). Maturity, reaching the goal God intends. Believers are called to grow up instead of staying at the starting point.

Baptisms and laying on of hands (6:2). Scripture speaks of baptism in water, in the Holy Spirit, and of suffering (Matthew 3:11; Luke 12:50; Acts 2:38), and some take the plural to include Jewish ritual washings. Laying on of hands appears in Scripture for imparting blessing and gifts, commissioning for service, and identification and confirmation (Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 13:1–3; 1 Timothy 4:14).

Partakers of the Holy Spirit (6:4). One of the real privileges shared by those the warning describes. The passage describes their experience within the gospel community without settling their inward standing.

Crucify again (6:6). Turning deliberately from Christ sides with those who rejected and shamed Him, and it turns from the only sacrifice that brings forgiveness.

Two immutable things (6:18). God’s promise and His oath. Both are unchangeable because God cannot lie.

Forerunner (6:20). One who goes ahead to open the way for others to follow. Jesus has entered God’s presence for His people.

focus: Hebrews 6 presses the dull hearers of Hebrews 5:11–14 to go on to maturity and warns them gravely about falling away after receiving great privileges. The writer then voices confidence in their love and rests their hope on God’s promise and oath, an anchor that enters behind the veil, where Jesus has gone as forerunner and High Priest forever.

sections.title: Go On to Maturity
sections.summary: Leaving the discussion of the elementary principles of Christ, the writer urges, “let us go on to perfection” (Hebrews 6:1), without laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, faith toward God, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. He adds, “And this we will do if God permits” (Hebrews 6:3).

sections.title: The Warning Against Falling Away
sections.summary: It is impossible to renew to repentance those who were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, became partakers of the Holy Spirit, and tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they fall away, since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God and put Him to an open shame. Land that drinks in the rain and bears useful herbs receives blessing from God, but land that bears thorns and briers is rejected and near to being cursed.

sections.title: Confident of Better Things
sections.summary: “But, beloved, we are confident of better things concerning you” (Hebrews 6:9), for God will not forget their labor of love shown toward His name as they ministered to the saints and still do. The writer wants each of them to show the same diligence to the end and to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

sections.title: God’s Promise Confirmed by an Oath
sections.summary: God promised to bless and multiply Abraham and, having no one greater to swear by, swore by Himself, and Abraham obtained the promise after he had patiently endured. In the same way God confirmed His counsel to the heirs of promise with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, those who have fled for refuge might have strong consolation.

sections.title: An Anchor Behind the Veil
sections.summary: This hope is “an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast” (Hebrews 6:19), and it enters the Presence behind the veil. There Jesus has entered for us as forerunner, having become High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

1.brief: Leaving behind the elementary teaching about Christ, the writer urges, “let us go on to perfection,” meaning maturity, without laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God. The basics remain the foundation, but believers are not meant to stay at the starting point.
1.explain: “let us go on to perfection” The call grows out of the rebuke in Hebrews 5:11–14. Perfection here is reaching the intended maturity of a disciple. The elementary teachings remain the foundation on which that growth depends. Repentance turns a person from dead works, deeds that yield no life before God, and faith turns that person toward the God who gives life.

2.brief: The foundation also includes the doctrine of baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. The plural baptisms point to baptism in water, in the Holy Spirit, and of suffering, and the laying on of hands serves to impart blessing, to commission people for service, and to express identification or confirmation. These first teachings support the Christian life, and the call is to build on them rather than keep relaying them.
2.explain:
“the doctrine of baptisms” Scripture speaks of immersion in water, baptism in the Holy Spirit, and Jesus’ baptism of suffering (Acts 2:38, Matthew 3:11, and Luke 12:50). These are part of the range the plural brings to mind.

“of laying on of hands” Scripture uses the act in imparting blessing, the Holy Spirit, gifts, or healing, in commissioning people for service, and in identifying or confirming a person or action. Acts 8:17 and 1 Timothy 4:14 illustrate impartation, Acts 13:2–3 shows commissioning, and Leviticus 1:4 shows identification with the offering. Laying on of hands is a real spiritual ministry, not an empty ceremony. It is practiced with prayer, humility, and the Holy Spirit’s guidance, ordinarily within the local church under its elders, and never in haste, as Paul warned Timothy: “Do not lay hands on anyone hastily” (1 Timothy 5:22). Resurrection and eternal judgment complete the list by placing this life under the promises and accountability of the age to come.
2.notes: Hebrews 9:10 uses the related Greek term for ritual washings. Some readers therefore include Jewish washings alongside Christian baptism in the plural here.

3.brief: “And this we will do if God permits,” the writer says, including himself in the call to grow. Progress toward maturity depends on God’s enabling as well as on the hearers’ response.
3.explain: “if God permits” The writer includes himself in the resolve to move forward. The congregation’s effort remains dependent on God. That dependence gives the warning that follows its seriousness.

4.brief: The writer begins a grave warning about those who were once enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit. He describes people who have received real and great privileges from God.
4.explain: “those who were once enlightened” The warning describes professing believers in the congregation who had received real spiritual privileges. They had been brought into the light of the gospel, had experienced the heavenly gift, and had shared in the Holy Spirit’s work. The writer describes what they received without pronouncing on their prior inward standing. The sentence begins with impossibility and reaches its conclusion in verse 6.

5.brief: The people described in this warning have also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come. They have experienced the goodness of God’s word and a foretaste of the power of the coming age.
5.explain: “the powers of the age to come” They had also experienced the goodness of God’s word and the powers that give a foretaste of the coming age. Together, verses 4 and 5 show how much light and grace these hearers had received. Hebrews makes the gravity of turning away clear by naming what they had actually shared in.

6.brief: If people who have been enlightened and have tasted God’s gifts in this way fall away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, “since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God, and put Him to an open shame.” Their falling away is a deliberate repudiation of Christ that sides with those who rejected and shamed Him and turns from the only sacrifice for sins.
6.explain: “to renew them again to repentance” Those who deliberately and decisively turn from Christ after receiving these privileges cannot be renewed again to repentance. By repudiating the Son they side with those who crucified and publicly shamed Him and reject the only sacrifice through which they could return (Hebrews 10:26). The consequence concerns settled rejection of Christ. A believer who grieves over sin and wants to come back can go to the High Priest for mercy and help (Hebrews 4:14–16).
6.notes: The NKJV puts the falling away in an if clause. The Greek lists falling away in the same grammatical sequence as the experiences in verses 4–5. Both ways of presenting the sentence leave the earlier inward standing of the people undescribed while naming the act that brings the warning to bear.

7.brief: Land that drinks in the frequent rain and then produces useful crops for those who farm it “receives blessing from God.” The rain falls on every field, but God’s blessing rests on the land whose crop answers the rain it received.
7.explain: “the earth which drinks in the rain” The first field repeatedly receives rain, then produces crops useful to those who cultivate it. God blesses that land. The image pictures a fruitful response to real privileges from God and prepares for the different crop the same rain can produce.

8.brief: But if land that drinks in the same rain bears thorns and briers, it is rejected and near to being cursed, “whose end is to be burned.” The rain is God’s good gift to both fields, and the difference lies in what each field produces; the thorns picture the response the warning has just described, in which people receive God’s gifts and then turn against the One who gave them.
8.explain: “if it bears thorns and briers” The thorns grow on ground that has received the same rain. The field is rejected, near to a curse, and ends by being burned. This is the warning of verses 4–6 in a picture: receiving great spiritual privileges offers no refuge from judgment when the response is settled rejection of the Son.

9.brief: “But, beloved, we are confident of better things concerning you,” the writer says, “things that accompany salvation,” even though he has spoken so severely. The warning is given in love, and it stands beside his genuine confidence in his hearers.
9.explain: “we are confident of better things concerning you” Beloved marks the writer’s affection as he turns from warning to encouragement. He expects things that accompany salvation, such as the love and service he will immediately name. His confidence gives the congregation reason to hear the warning as an appeal to keep going.

10.brief: God is not unjust to forget their work and labor of love shown toward His name, in that they have served the saints and are still serving them. Their love for fellow believers is fruit God sees and remembers.
10.explain: “your work and labor of love” God justly remembers the service the hearers have given to His people and still give. Their care for the saints is love shown toward His name. It supplies a concrete reason for the writer’s confidence in verse 9.

11.brief: The writer wants each one of them to show the same diligence “to the full assurance of hope until the end.” The earnestness they have shown in love is needed in holding on to hope until the finish.
11.explain: “the full assurance of hope until the end” The writer wants every individual to show the same earnestness in hope that the congregation has shown in service. Assurance has an object: God’s promise, which the writer is about to confirm. The call is for that confident hope to endure to the end.

12.brief: The writer does not want his hearers to become sluggish but to imitate those who “through faith and patience inherit the promises.” Faith that keeps trusting and patience that keeps waiting are the way God’s people come into what He has promised.
12.explain: “through faith and patience inherit the promises” Faith keeps trusting God, and patience stays with His promise through the wait. The remedy for becoming sluggish is to imitate people whose lives display both. Abraham is the first example the writer gives.

13.brief: When God made His promise to Abraham, He swore by Himself, because He could swear by no one greater. God bound His promise to His own unchanging name.
13.explain: “He swore by Himself” When God confirmed His promise to Abraham, He could invoke no one greater than Himself. His own character backs His oath. Genesis 22:15–18 places the oath after the testing of Abraham, when Isaac had already been born and Abraham had offered him on the altar.

14.brief: God’s sworn promise to Abraham was, “Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.” The doubled wording underlines the certainty and abundance of the blessing God pledged.
14.explain: “Surely blessing I will bless you” God promises both to bless Abraham and to multiply his descendants. The repeated wording gives the sworn blessing and multiplication emphatic force. Abraham’s hope for a family rested on the God who spoke.

15.brief: After Abraham had patiently endured, “he obtained the promise,” receiving the son God had promised and then hearing God confirm His blessing with an oath after he offered Isaac. That real reception was the first stage of a promise whose fuller fulfillment Abraham’s family still awaited, as Hebrews 11:13 later explains.
15.explain: “after he had patiently endured” Abraham waited about twenty-five years for the son God promised. He was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4) and one hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 21:5). In Isaac he received the son through whom the promised family would come. Years later, after Abraham offered Isaac, God confirmed His blessing with the oath quoted in Hebrews 6:14 (Genesis 22:15–18). The birth of Isaac and the sworn confirmation were real receiving of the promise, yet the family’s full inheritance still lay ahead (Hebrews 11:13). Abraham shows what Hebrews means by receiving a promise through patient faith while the whole fulfillment remains future.

16.brief: Among people, an oath is sworn by someone greater, and it settles every dispute by confirming what was said. Hebrews uses this common practice to explain why God’s oath matters.
16.explain: “an oath for confirmation” People commonly appeal to someone greater when they swear, and the oath settles what is in dispute. Hebrews uses that familiar practice to explain why God chose to give an oath in addition to His promise.

17.brief: Wanting to show the heirs of promise even more clearly that His purpose would not change, God confirmed His promise with an oath. God went beyond what was necessary so that His people could be fully sure of Him.
17.explain: “the immutability of His counsel” God used the oath to show the heirs that His purpose does not change. The additional confirmation serves the people who need encouragement. The promise is as reliable as the God who swore to fulfill it.

18.brief: By two unchangeable things, God’s promise and His oath, “in which it is impossible for God to lie,” those who have fled to Him for refuge have strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before them. Their confidence rests on the character of the God who cannot lie.
18.explain: “two immutable things” The promise and oath are both unchangeable because God cannot lie. They strongly encourage those who have fled to Him for refuge to hold firmly to the hope He sets before them. The certainty of their hope rests in His truthfulness.

19.brief: The hope set before believers is “an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast,” and it reaches into the Presence behind the veil. The believer’s hope is fastened in God’s own presence, where nothing can tear it loose.
19.explain: “an anchor of the soul” Hope holds believers steady because it reaches into God’s presence behind the veil. The ordinary anchor holds by taking hold of something firm beyond the vessel. Hebrews pictures our hope taking hold where Jesus already is, which explains why it is both sure and steadfast.

20.brief: Jesus has entered behind the veil for us as our forerunner, having become High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Where He has gone ahead, His people’s hope is secured and their way is opened, and the mention of Melchizedek leads into chapter 7.
20.explain: “the forerunner has entered for us” Jesus has entered God’s presence on our behalf and ahead of us. As High Priest forever in Melchizedek’s order, He remains there for His people. His entrance secures their hope and opens the way for them to follow.
